_comment: Math tutorials v1. 156 entries — kid-tier core (~113) + adult-tier additions (~43). Matched via findByTriggers scorer. Walker names reference functions in js/mathWalkers.js.

triggers: how does addition with carrying work
tutorials.title: Addition With Carrying
tutorials.body:
When you add two digits and the answer is 10 or more, you write the ones digit and 'carry' the tens digit to the next column. Stack the numbers by place value, add right to left.

Example: 47 + 28. 7 + 8 = 15. Write 5, carry the 1. Then 4 + 2 + 1 (carried) = 7. Answer: 75.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '47 + 28'.

tutorials.title: Subtraction With Borrowing
tutorials.body:
When the top digit is smaller than the bottom digit, you 'borrow' 10 from the next column to the left. That column loses 1, and the current column gains 10.

Example: 52 - 27. 2 - 7 doesn't work, so borrow: the 5 becomes 4, and the 2 becomes 12. 12 - 7 = 5. Then 4 - 2 = 2. Answer: 25.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '52 - 27'.

tutorials.title: Times Tables Intuition
tutorials.formula: a × b = a added b times
tutorials.body:
Multiplication is repeated addition. 4 × 3 means 'four, three times' — that's 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. You can also picture it as a rectangle: 4 rows of 3 dots = 12 dots.

The order doesn't matter: 4 × 3 = 3 × 4. That's why memorizing one half of the table covers the other half too.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '7 × 8'.

tutorials.title: Long Multiplication
tutorials.body:
Multiply the top number by each digit of the bottom number, one at a time. Each new row shifts left by one place. Then add the rows.

Example: 23 × 45. First 23 × 5 = 115. Then 23 × 4 = 92, but shifted left makes it 920. Add: 115 + 920 = 1035.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '23 × 45'.

tutorials.title: Long Division
tutorials.body:
Divide-multiply-subtract-bring-down, repeat. Take the leftmost digits of the dividend that fit the divisor, divide, write the answer on top, multiply back, subtract, then bring down the next digit.

Example: 156 ÷ 4. 4 into 15 is 3 (remainder 3). Bring down the 6 to make 36. 4 into 36 is 9. Answer: 39.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'long division 156 ÷ 4'.

tutorials.title: Order of Operations (PEMDAS)
tutorials.body:
Do operations in this order: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division (left to right), Addition/Subtraction (left to right). PEMDAS in the US, BODMAS in the UK — same idea.

Example: 2 + 3 × 4. Multiplication first: 3 × 4 = 12. Then add: 2 + 12 = 14. Not 20.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '2 + 3 × 4'.

tutorials.title: Negative Numbers
tutorials.body:
Negative numbers are less than zero. On a number line they live to the left of 0. Think of money owed, or temperatures below freezing.

Rules: subtracting a negative is the same as adding (5 - (-3) = 8). Negative × negative = positive (-2 × -3 = 6). Negative × positive = negative.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '-7 + 12'.

tutorials.title: Absolute Value
tutorials.body: Absolute value is how far a number is from zero, ignoring direction. |5| = 5 and |-5| = 5. It's always zero or positive.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is |-12|'.

tutorials.title: Rounding Numbers
tutorials.body:
Pick the place you're rounding to. Look at the digit just to the right. If it's 5 or more, round up. If it's 4 or less, round down. Everything to the right becomes zero (or drops off after a decimal).

Example: round 347 to the nearest ten. The digit to the right of the tens is 7, so round up: 350. Round 23.4 to the nearest whole = 23.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'round 268 to the nearest ten'.

tutorials.title: Estimating
tutorials.body:
Estimating means getting close to the answer fast, without doing exact math. Round each number to something easy, then compute. Great for checking if your real answer is reasonable.

Example: 412 + 297. Round to 400 + 300 = 700. The exact answer (709) is very close, so 700 was a solid estimate.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'estimate 489 + 612'.

tutorials.title: Place Value
tutorials.body:
Each digit in a number has a value based on its position. Right to left: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, and so on. The number 357 means 3 hundreds + 5 tens + 7 ones.

Move a digit one slot left and its value multiplies by 10. That's why 30 is ten times bigger than 3.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what's the place value of the 4 in 2,401'.

tutorials.title: Scientific Notation
tutorials.body:
Scientific notation writes huge or tiny numbers as a small number times a power of 10. The exponent says how many places to slide the decimal point. Positive = big, negative = small.

Example: 3,000,000 = 3 × 10⁶. 0.00042 = 4.2 × 10⁻⁴. Easier to read than counting zeros.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'write 0.00042 in scientific notation'.

tutorials.title: Square Roots
tutorials.formula: √x = the number that squares to x
tutorials.body:
A square root undoes squaring. √9 = 3 because 3 × 3 = 9. √25 = 5 because 5 × 5 = 25.

Most numbers don't have a clean square root — √2 ≈ 1.414... Those decimals never end or repeat. We call them irrational numbers.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'square root of 144'.

tutorials.title: Perfect Squares
tutorials.body: A perfect square is a whole number you get by squaring an integer: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, 144... Their square roots are whole numbers.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'is 169 a perfect square'.

tutorials.title: Cube Roots
tutorials.formula: ∛x = the number that cubes to x
tutorials.body:
A cube root undoes cubing. ∛8 = 2 because 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. ∛27 = 3 because 3 × 3 × 3 = 27.

Unlike square roots, cube roots of negatives are fine: ∛(-8) = -2.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'cube root of 125'.

tutorials.title: Fraction
tutorials.body: A fraction is a part of a whole. The bottom (denominator) is how many equal pieces the whole is cut into. The top (numerator) is how many pieces you have. 3/4 means 'three out of four equal pieces'.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is 1/2 + 1/4'.

triggers: top and bottom of a fraction
tutorials.title: Numerator and Denominator
tutorials.body: Numerator is the top of a fraction (how many pieces you have). Denominator is the bottom (how many pieces the whole is cut into). In 5/8, the numerator is 5 and the denominator is 8.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is 2/3 simplified'.

triggers: how can two fractions be equal
tutorials.title: Equivalent Fractions
tutorials.body:
Two fractions are equivalent if they represent the same amount. Multiply (or divide) both the top and bottom by the same number and you get an equivalent fraction.

Example: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 50/100. All are 'half'.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'is 4/6 equal to 2/3'.

tutorials.title: Simplifying Fractions
tutorials.body:
To simplify, divide the top and bottom by their greatest common divisor (GCD). The fraction is in 'lowest terms' when the only number that divides both is 1.

Example: 8/12. GCD(8,12) = 4. Divide both: 8/12 = 2/3.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'simplify 15/35'.

tutorials.title: Adding Fractions With the Same Denominator
tutorials.body:
When the bottoms match, just add the tops and keep the bottom. The pieces are the same size, so you're just counting how many you have.

Example: 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '2/7 + 3/7'.

tutorials.title: Adding Fractions With Different Denominators
tutorials.body:
Find a common denominator (any number both bottoms divide into — usually the least common multiple). Convert each fraction, then add the tops.

Example: 1/3 + 1/4. Common denominator is 12. 1/3 = 4/12 and 1/4 = 3/12. Sum: 7/12.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '1/3 + 1/4'.

tutorials.title: Subtracting Fractions
tutorials.body:
Same rules as adding — get a common denominator, then subtract the tops. Keep the bottom.

Example: 3/4 - 1/6. Common denominator 12. 3/4 = 9/12, 1/6 = 2/12. Answer: 7/12.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '3/4 - 1/6'.

tutorials.title: Multiplying Fractions
tutorials.body:
Multiply the tops together and the bottoms together. No common denominator needed. Simplify at the end.

Example: 2/3 × 3/5 = 6/15 = 2/5.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '2/3 × 3/5'.

tutorials.title: Dividing Fractions (Flip and Multiply)
tutorials.body:
To divide by a fraction, flip the second one (the reciprocal) and multiply. 'Keep, change, flip.'

Example: 1/2 ÷ 3/4 = 1/2 × 4/3 = 4/6 = 2/3.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '1/2 ÷ 3/4'.

tutorials.title: Mixed Numbers and Improper Fractions
tutorials.body:
A mixed number like 2 3/4 means 2 + 3/4. An improper fraction has a top bigger than its bottom, like 11/4.

To convert 2 3/4 to improper: 2 × 4 + 3 = 11, over 4 → 11/4. To go back: 11 ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 3 → 2 3/4.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'convert 7/3 to a mixed number'.

tutorials.title: Fractions and Decimals
tutorials.body:
A fraction is just division. Divide the top by the bottom to get the decimal. 3/4 → 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75.

To go the other way, write the decimal over its place value and simplify. 0.6 = 6/10 = 3/5.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is 5/8 as a decimal'.

tutorials.title: Fractions and Percents
tutorials.body:
Convert a fraction to a decimal, then multiply by 100. 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%.

Going the other way: divide the percent by 100 and simplify. 40% = 40/100 = 2/5.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is 7/20 as a percent'.

tutorials.title: Comparing Fractions
tutorials.body:
Give them a common denominator, then compare the tops. Or convert each to a decimal and compare.

Example: is 3/5 or 2/3 bigger? Common denominator 15: 3/5 = 9/15 and 2/3 = 10/15. So 2/3 is bigger.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'is 5/8 or 3/5 bigger'.

tutorials.title: Ordering Fractions
tutorials.body:
Find a common denominator for all of them, then sort by the tops. Or convert each to a decimal and sort.

Example: order 1/2, 2/5, 3/4. Common denominator 20: 10/20, 8/20, 15/20. Smallest to largest: 2/5, 1/2, 3/4.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'order 1/3, 1/4, 2/5'.

triggers: how to solve fraction word problems
tutorials.title: Fraction Word Problems
tutorials.body:
Read it twice. Spot the fractions and the question. 'Of' usually means multiply. 'Left' or 'remaining' usually means subtract.

Example: A pizza has 8 slices. You eat 3/8 and your friend eats 1/4. How much is left? 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8 eaten, so 3/8 remains.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: 'half of 24 is what'.

tutorials.title: How Percentages Work
tutorials.body:
A percent is just a fraction with 100 on the bottom. 25% means 25 out of 100, or 25/100 = 0.25. To find 25% of something, multiply by 0.25.

Example: 25% of 80 = 0.25 × 80 = 20.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '15% of 60'.

triggers: how to find percent of a number
what is x percent of y
tutorials.title: Finding X% of Y
tutorials.body:
Convert the percent to a decimal (divide by 100), then multiply.

Example: 30% of 150 = 0.30 × 150 = 45. Quick mental trick: 10% of 150 is 15, so 30% is three of those = 45.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '20% of 250'.

tutorials.title: Percent Change
tutorials.body:
Subtract old from new, divide by old, multiply by 100. Positive = increase, negative = decrease.

Example: price went from $40 to $50. (50 − 40)/40 = 0.25 = 25% increase.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'percent change from 80 to 100'.

tutorials.title: Calculating a Discount
tutorials.body:
Multiply the original price by (1 minus the discount as a decimal). Or just find the discount amount and subtract.

Example: $80 with 25% off. 80 × 0.75 = $60. Or: 80 × 0.25 = $20 off, so 80 − 20 = $60.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '30% off $120'.

triggers: what is the total with tax
tutorials.title: Sales Tax
tutorials.body:
Multiply the price by the tax rate as a decimal to get the tax amount. Add it to the price for the total.

Example: $50 item, 8% tax. Tax = 50 × 0.08 = $4. Total = $54.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '7% tax on $80'.

tutorials.title: Calculating a Tip
tutorials.body:
Move the decimal one place left to get 10%. Double that for 20%. Halve the 10% for 15%.

Example: $48 bill. 10% = $4.80. 20% = $9.60. 15% = $4.80 + $2.40 = $7.20.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '18% tip on $60'.

tutorials.title: Percent Error
tutorials.body:
Used in science to say how far off a measurement is. Take the absolute difference, divide by the true value, multiply by 100.

Example: you measure 9.6 g, real value is 10 g. |9.6 − 10|/10 = 0.04 = 4% error.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'percent error if I measured 48 and actual is 50'.

triggers: how to turn a fraction into a percent
tutorials.title: Fraction to Percent
tutorials.body:
Divide top by bottom, then multiply by 100. Or scale the fraction so the bottom is 100.

Example: 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%. Or: 3/4 = 75/100 = 75%.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is 9/20 as a percent'.

triggers: how to turn a decimal into a percent
tutorials.title: Decimal to Percent
tutorials.body:
Move the decimal point two places to the right. That's it.

Example: 0.45 = 45%. 0.07 = 7%. 1.2 = 120%.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is 0.08 as a percent'.

tutorials.title: Compound Percent (Compound Interest)
tutorials.body:
Each round of growth applies to the previous total, not the original. Small percents compound into big growth over time.

Example: $100 at 10% per year for 3 years. Year 1: $110. Year 2: $121. Year 3: $133.10. Not just $130.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '$500 at 5% for 4 years compound'.

tutorials.title: Variable
tutorials.body: A variable is a letter that stands in for a number we don't know yet (or that can change). In x + 3 = 7, x is a variable. We solve to find that x = 4.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'solve x + 3 = 7'.

tutorials.title: What '=' Really Means
tutorials.body:
The equals sign means 'both sides are the same'. It's a balance. Whatever you do to one side, you have to do to the other to keep it balanced.

Example: in x + 3 = 7, the stuff on the left equals 7. If you subtract 3 from both sides, x = 4.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is x in x + 5 = 12'.

triggers: what does it mean to balance an equation
tutorials.title: Balancing an Equation
tutorials.body:
An equation is like a scale. To keep it balanced, do the same thing to both sides — add, subtract, multiply, divide, whatever.

Example: 2x + 1 = 9. Subtract 1 from both sides: 2x = 8. Divide both sides by 2: x = 4.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'solve 2x + 1 = 9'.

triggers: how to solve one step equations
tutorials.title: One-Step Equations
tutorials.body:
Do the opposite of whatever's happening to x. Added? Subtract. Multiplied? Divide.

Examples: x + 5 = 12 → subtract 5 → x = 7. 4x = 20 → divide by 4 → x = 5.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'solve 4x = 20'.

triggers: how to solve two step equations
tutorials.title: Two-Step Equations
tutorials.body:
Undo addition/subtraction first, then undo multiplication/division. Reverse of PEMDAS.

Example: 2x + 3 = 11. Subtract 3: 2x = 8. Divide by 2: x = 4.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'solve 3x − 5 = 16'.

tutorials.title: Distributive Property
tutorials.body:
Multiplying a number by a sum is the same as multiplying it by each piece, then adding.

Example: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. 2(5 + 7) = 10 + 14 = 24 (same as 2 × 12).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'expand 5(x + 3)'.

tutorials.title: Combining Like Terms
tutorials.body:
Like terms have the same variable raised to the same power. You can add or subtract their coefficients. Constants combine with constants.

Example: 3x + 5 + 2x − 1 = 5x + 4. (3x and 2x combine; 5 and −1 combine.)
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'simplify 4x + 7 − x + 3'.

tutorials.title: Exponent Rules
tutorials.body:
Same base, multiplying: add exponents (x³ × x² = x⁵). Same base, dividing: subtract exponents (x⁵ ÷ x² = x³). Power of a power: multiply exponents ((x²)³ = x⁶).

Anything to the 0 power is 1. Negative exponents flip to the bottom: x⁻² = 1/x².
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is x^4 × x^3'.

tutorials.title: Factoring Out a Common Factor
tutorials.body:
Find the biggest number (and variable) that divides every term, pull it outside parentheses. It's the reverse of the distributive property.

Example: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3). 4x² + 6x = 2x(2x + 3).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'factor 8x + 12'.

tutorials.title: Factoring Quadratics (a = 1)
tutorials.formula: x² + bx + c = (x + p)(x + q) where p+q=b, pq=c
tutorials.body:
Find two numbers that add to b and multiply to c. Those go inside the parentheses.

Example: x² + 5x + 6. Two numbers that add to 5 and multiply to 6: 2 and 3. So x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'factor x² + 7x + 12'.

triggers: ax squared plus bx plus c
tutorials.title: The Quadratic Formula
tutorials.body:
For any equation in the form ax² + bx + c = 0, this formula gives the solutions. The ± means you usually get two answers.

Example: x² − 5x + 6 = 0. a=1, b=−5, c=6. x = (5 ± √(25−24))/2 = (5 ± 1)/2 → x = 3 or x = 2.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0'.

tutorials.title: FOIL — Multiplying Binomials
tutorials.formula: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd
tutorials.body:
FOIL = First, Outer, Inner, Last. Multiply each pair from the two binomials, then combine like terms.

Example: (x + 2)(x + 3) = x² + 3x + 2x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'expand (x + 4)(x + 5)'.

tutorials.title: Slope
tutorials.body:
Slope is how steep a line is — rise over run. Pick two points on the line. Subtract the y values for rise. Subtract the x values for run. Divide.

Example: points (1, 2) and (4, 8). Slope = (8−2)/(4−1) = 6/3 = 2. The line rises 2 for every 1 you go right.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'slope between (0,0) and (3,6)'.

triggers: what does y = mx + b mean
tutorials.title: Slope-Intercept Form (y = mx + b)
tutorials.body:
Every straight line can be written y = mx + b. m is the slope (steepness). b is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis).

Example: y = 2x + 3. Slope 2, crosses the y-axis at 3. To plot: start at (0, 3), then go up 2 and right 1.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'graph y = 2x + 3'.

triggers: what is a system of equations
tutorials.title: Systems of Linear Equations
tutorials.body:
Two equations with two unknowns. The solution is the point (x, y) that satisfies both. Solve by substitution or elimination.

Example: x + y = 5 and x − y = 1. Add the two equations: 2x = 6, so x = 3. Then y = 2.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'solve x + y = 5 and x − y = 1'.

tutorials.title: Perimeter of a Rectangle
tutorials.body:
Perimeter is the distance around the outside. Add length and width, double it. Or add all four sides.

Example: rectangle 5 by 3. P = 2(5 + 3) = 16.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'perimeter of a 7 by 4 rectangle'.

triggers: how to find perimeter of triangle
tutorials.title: Perimeter of a Triangle
tutorials.body:
Just add up the three sides.

Example: triangle with sides 3, 4, 5. Perimeter = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'perimeter of triangle with sides 6, 8, 10'.

tutorials.title: Circumference of a Circle
tutorials.body:
Circumference is the distance around the circle. Multiply the radius by 2π, or just the diameter by π. π ≈ 3.14159.

Example: radius 5. C = 2 × π × 5 ≈ 31.42.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'circumference of a circle with radius 7'.

tutorials.title: Area of a Rectangle
tutorials.body:
Length times width. Area is measured in square units (how many 1×1 squares would fit inside).

Example: 5 by 3 rectangle. A = 5 × 3 = 15.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'area of a 7 by 4 rectangle'.

tutorials.title: Area of a Triangle
tutorials.body:
Half of base times height. The height is the straight-up distance from the base to the opposite point (not the slanted side).

Example: base 8, height 5. A = ½ × 8 × 5 = 20.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'area of a triangle with base 10 and height 6'.

tutorials.title: Area of a Circle
tutorials.body:
Square the radius, multiply by π. π is roughly 3.14.

Example: radius 5. A = π × 25 ≈ 78.54.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'area of a circle with radius 7'.

triggers: how to find area of trapezoid
tutorials.title: Area of a Trapezoid
tutorials.body:
Average the two parallel sides, multiply by the height between them.

Example: bases 6 and 10, height 4. A = ½ × (6 + 10) × 4 = ½ × 16 × 4 = 32.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'area of a trapezoid with bases 5 and 9 and height 4'.

triggers: how to find area of parallelogram
tutorials.title: Area of a Parallelogram
tutorials.body:
Base times height — same as a rectangle. The height is the straight-up distance, not the slanted side.

Example: base 8, height 5. A = 40.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'area of a parallelogram base 10 height 6'.

tutorials.title: Volume of a Cube
tutorials.body:
Cube the side length. A cube has all sides equal.

Example: side 4. V = 4³ = 64.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'volume of a cube with side 5'.

tutorials.title: Volume of a Rectangular Prism
tutorials.body:
Length × width × height. Measured in cubic units.

Example: 3 × 4 × 5 = 60.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'volume of a 2 by 3 by 4 box'.

triggers: how to find volume of cylinder
tutorials.title: Volume of a Cylinder
tutorials.body:
Area of the circle on top × the height. Pretend it's a stack of circles.

Example: radius 3, height 10. V = π × 9 × 10 ≈ 282.74.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'volume of a cylinder radius 5 height 8'.

triggers: how to find volume of sphere
tutorials.title: Volume of a Sphere
tutorials.body:
Four-thirds π r cubed. A sphere is round in every direction (a ball).

Example: radius 3. V = (4/3) × π × 27 ≈ 113.10.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'volume of a sphere with radius 5'.

triggers: how to find volume of cone
tutorials.title: Volume of a Cone
tutorials.body:
One-third of a cylinder with the same base and height. The pointy top eats two-thirds of the space.

Example: radius 3, height 6. V = (1/3) × π × 9 × 6 ≈ 56.55.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'volume of a cone radius 4 height 9'.

triggers: what is a squared plus b squared
tutorials.title: Pythagorean Theorem
tutorials.body:
In a right triangle, the two short sides squared and added equal the long side (hypotenuse) squared.

Example: legs 3 and 4. 9 + 16 = 25. Hypotenuse = √25 = 5. That's the famous 3-4-5 triangle.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'hypotenuse if legs are 6 and 8'.

tutorials.title: Special Right Triangles
tutorials.body:
Two right triangles show up so often they have memorized side ratios. 45-45-90: sides 1 : 1 : √2. 30-60-90: sides 1 : √3 : 2.

Example: a 45-45-90 with legs of 5 has hypotenuse 5√2. A 30-60-90 with short leg 1 has long leg √3 and hypotenuse 2.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'sides of a 30-60-90 triangle with short leg 4'.

tutorials.title: Similar Triangles
tutorials.body:
Similar triangles have the same shape but different sizes. Their angles match, and their sides are in proportion.

Example: one triangle has sides 3, 4, 5. Another has 6, 8, 10. Same shape, doubled. They're similar.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'are triangles 3-4-5 and 9-12-15 similar'.

tutorials.title: Congruent Triangles
tutorials.body:
Congruent triangles are the same shape AND the same size. You can match them up exactly by sliding, rotating, or flipping.

Prove it with SSS (all three sides match), SAS (two sides and the angle between), or ASA (two angles and the side between).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the difference between similar and congruent'.

triggers: what are the types of angles
tutorials.title: Types of Angles
tutorials.body:
Acute = less than 90°. Right = exactly 90° (square corner). Obtuse = between 90° and 180°. Straight = exactly 180° (a flat line). Reflex = more than 180°.

A 45° angle is acute. A doorframe corner is right. A reclining lawn chair makes an obtuse angle.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'is a 75 degree angle acute'.

tutorials.title: Triangle Angle Sum
tutorials.body:
The three angles inside any triangle add up to 180°. Always.

Example: if two angles are 70° and 60°, the third is 180 − 70 − 60 = 50°.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'third angle of a triangle if two are 45 and 90'.

triggers: how many degrees in a polygon
tutorials.title: Interior Angles of a Polygon
tutorials.body:
For a polygon with n sides, the interior angles add up to (n − 2) × 180°. You can split any polygon into (n − 2) triangles.

Example: quadrilateral (n=4): (4−2) × 180 = 360°. Pentagon (n=5): 540°. Hexagon (n=6): 720°.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'interior angles of a hexagon'.

tutorials.title: SOH-CAH-TOA
tutorials.body:
Mnemonic for trig in a right triangle. SOH: Sine = Opposite / Hypotenuse. CAH: Cosine = Adjacent / Hypotenuse. TOA: Tangent = Opposite / Adjacent.

'Opposite' is across from the angle. 'Adjacent' is next to it (and not the hypotenuse). 'Hypotenuse' is the longest side, across from the right angle.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is sine of 30 degrees'.

triggers: what do sin and cos mean
tutorials.title: Sine, Cosine, Tangent (Plain Language)
tutorials.body:
They're three ways to relate an angle of a right triangle to its sides. Pick any angle (not the 90°). Sine is how 'tall' the triangle is for its long side, cosine is how 'wide', tangent is tall over wide.

Calculators have sin, cos, tan buttons. Don't memorize values — memorize what they mean.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'when do I use sine vs cosine'.

tutorials.title: Unit Circle Basics
tutorials.body:
Draw a circle of radius 1 at the origin. For any angle θ measured from the positive x-axis, the point on the circle is (cos θ, sin θ). That's the whole trick.

This lets sin and cos work for any angle, not just acute ones in a right triangle. Negatives, big angles, full spins — all fine.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is cos of 90 degrees'.

tutorials.title: Sin/Cos at Common Angles
tutorials.body:
Worth memorizing: sin(0°)=0, sin(30°)=½, sin(45°)=√2/2, sin(60°)=√3/2, sin(90°)=1. Cosine is the reverse list: cos(0°)=1, cos(30°)=√3/2, cos(45°)=√2/2, cos(60°)=½, cos(90°)=0.

Tangent is sin/cos: tan(45°)=1, tan(0°)=0, tan(90°) is undefined.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is sin of 60'.

triggers: what is the law of sines
tutorials.title: Law of Sines
tutorials.formula: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
tutorials.body:
For any triangle (not just right ones), each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle gives the same ratio.

Use it when you know two angles and a side, or two sides and an angle opposite one of them.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'when do I use law of sines'.

triggers: what is the law of cosines
tutorials.title: Law of Cosines
tutorials.body:
Generalization of the Pythagorean theorem for any triangle. If C is 90°, cos C = 0 and you're back to a² + b² = c².

Use it when you know two sides and the included angle, or all three sides and you need an angle.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'when do I use law of cosines'.

triggers: law of sines vs law of cosines
when to use law of sines or cosines
tutorials.title: Which Trig Law to Use
tutorials.body:
Law of Sines: you have a side and its opposite angle paired up. Good for two angles + a side, or two sides + a non-included angle.

Law of Cosines: you have two sides and the angle between them, or all three sides and want an angle. No side-angle pair needed.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the law of cosines'.

tutorials.title: Mean (Average)
tutorials.body:
The mean is the average. Add all the numbers, divide by how many there are.

Example: 2, 4, 6, 8. Sum = 20. Count = 4. Mean = 5.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'average of 3, 7, 8, 10'.

tutorials.title: Median
tutorials.body:
Median is the middle number. Sort the list, then pick the one in the middle. If there are two in the middle, take their average.

Example: 1, 3, 4, 7, 9 → median is 4. For 1, 3, 4, 7 → middle two are 3 and 4, so median is 3.5.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'median of 2, 5, 8, 11, 14'.

tutorials.title: Mode
tutorials.body:
Mode is the number that appears most often. A list can have one mode, several, or none.

Example: 2, 4, 4, 7, 9 → mode is 4. For 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4 → modes are 2 and 3 (bimodal).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'mode of 5, 5, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8'.

tutorials.title: Range
tutorials.body: The range is the biggest number minus the smallest. It tells you how spread out the data is. Example: 3, 7, 12, 18 → range is 18 − 3 = 15.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'range of 4, 9, 11, 22'.

tutorials.title: Variance and Standard Deviation
tutorials.body:
Both measure how spread out data is from the mean. Standard deviation is the typical 'distance' from the average. Variance is just standard deviation squared.

Low stdev: everyone scores near the average. High stdev: scores all over the place. Stdev has the same units as the data; variance is in squared units.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is standard deviation'.

triggers: how do outliers affect the mean
tutorials.title: How Outliers Affect Mean vs Median
tutorials.body:
An outlier is a number far from the rest. They yank the mean toward themselves but barely move the median.

Example: 4, 5, 6, 7, 100. Mean = 24.4 (way off). Median = 6 (still reasonable). That's why median is often better for skewed data like income.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is an outlier'.

tutorials.title: Histogram
tutorials.body:
A histogram is a bar chart for numerical data. The x-axis is grouped into intervals (bins), and each bar's height shows how many data points fall in that bin.

Use it to see the shape of a distribution — bell-shaped, skewed, two-humped, flat.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a normal distribution'.

tutorials.title: Box Plot
tutorials.body:
A box plot shows the median, the middle 50% of the data (the box), and the full range (the whiskers). Outliers show up as dots beyond the whiskers.

Great for comparing several groups side by side.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the median'.

tutorials.title: Correlation vs Causation
tutorials.body:
Correlation: two things move together. Causation: one actually causes the other. Just because A and B happen together doesn't mean A causes B — they might both be caused by something else.

Example: ice cream sales and shark attacks both go up in summer. Ice cream doesn't cause shark attacks. Hot weather causes both.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a confounding variable'.

triggers: what is a population in stats
tutorials.title: Sample vs Population
tutorials.body:
Population: everyone or everything you care about. Sample: a smaller group you actually measure. Stats is the art of using a sample to guess about a population.

Example: population = all voters. Sample = the 1,000 people the pollster called. The sample's stats estimate the population's.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is sampling bias'.

tutorials.title: Probability
tutorials.body:
Probability is the chance of something happening, on a scale from 0 (never) to 1 (always). Count the outcomes you want, divide by all possible outcomes.

Example: rolling a 4 on a fair die. One favorable outcome (a 4), six possible. P = 1/6 ≈ 0.167 or 16.7%.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'probability of flipping heads'.

tutorials.title: Sample Space
tutorials.body: The sample space is the set of every possible outcome of an experiment. For a coin flip: {heads, tails}. For a die: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'sample space of two coin flips'.

tutorials.title: Independent Events
tutorials.body:
Two events are independent if one doesn't affect the other. Multiply their probabilities to find the chance both happen.

Example: flip two coins. P(both heads) = ½ × ½ = ¼.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'probability of two heads in a row'.

tutorials.title: Dependent Events
tutorials.body:
Events are dependent if one changes the probability of the next. Common in 'without replacement' problems.

Example: draw 2 cards from a 52-card deck without replacement. P(first ace) = 4/52. P(second ace given first was an ace) = 3/51. P(both aces) = (4/52)(3/51).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'probability of drawing two aces in a row'.

tutorials.title: Compound Probability (And/Or)
tutorials.body:
AND (both happen): multiply. OR (either happens): add, then subtract the overlap so you don't double-count.

Example: rolling a die. P(even OR > 4) = P(even) + P(>4) − P(both). 3/6 + 2/6 − 1/6 = 4/6 = 2/3.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'probability of rolling a 6 or an odd number'.

tutorials.title: Conditional Probability
tutorials.body:
P(A|B) means 'probability of A given that B happened'. You're shrinking the sample space to just the outcomes where B is true.

Example: P(rolled a 2 | rolled an even number). Even outcomes are {2,4,6}, and 2 is one of them. P = 1/3.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'probability it rained given the grass is wet'.

tutorials.title: Permutations vs Combinations
tutorials.body:
Permutation: order matters (like a race podium). Combination: order doesn't (like picking a committee).

Example: from 5 people, how many ways to pick a top-3 ranked list? Permutations: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60. How many unordered groups of 3? Combinations: 60 / 6 = 10 (divide by 3! to remove the orderings).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how many ways to pick 2 from 5'.

tutorials.title: Expected Value
tutorials.body:
Expected value is the long-run average payoff. Multiply each outcome by its probability, then add them up.

Example: a game pays $10 with probability 1/4, otherwise $0. E = $10 × ¼ + $0 × ¾ = $2.50. If the entry fee is more than $2.50, don't play.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'expected value of rolling a die'.

tutorials.title: Prime Number
tutorials.body: A prime is a whole number greater than 1 with no divisors other than 1 and itself. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13... 1 is not prime by definition. 91 looks prime but isn't (91 = 7 × 13).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'is 97 prime'.

tutorials.title: Prime Factorization
tutorials.body:
Every whole number > 1 can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way. Build a factor tree: keep splitting until every leaf is prime.

Example: 60 = 2 × 30 = 2 × 2 × 15 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. Prime factorization of 60 is 2² × 3 × 5.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'prime factorization of 84'.

tutorials.title: Greatest Common Divisor (GCD)
tutorials.body:
The GCD of two numbers is the largest number that divides both. Find prime factorizations, multiply the common primes (taking the smaller power of each).

Example: GCD(24, 36). 24 = 2³ × 3, 36 = 2² × 3². Common: 2² × 3 = 12.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'gcd of 18 and 24'.

tutorials.title: Least Common Multiple (LCM)
tutorials.formula: LCM(a, b) = a × b / GCD(a, b)
tutorials.body:
The LCM is the smallest number that both numbers divide into. Useful for adding fractions (find a common denominator).

Example: LCM(4, 6). Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12. Multiples of 6: 6, 12. LCM = 12.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'lcm of 6 and 8'.

triggers: how to tell if a number is divisible
tutorials.title: Divisibility Rules
tutorials.body:
Quick checks without dividing. By 2: last digit is even. By 3: digit sum is divisible by 3. By 5: ends in 0 or 5. By 9: digit sum is divisible by 9. By 10: ends in 0.

Example: 234. Digit sum 9 → divisible by 3 and 9. Last digit 4 → divisible by 2. Not divisible by 5 or 10.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'is 1287 divisible by 3'.

tutorials.title: Metric vs Imperial
tutorials.body:
Metric: based on 10s. Easy to convert (just slide the decimal). Used almost everywhere — meters, kilograms, liters, Celsius.

Imperial: based on whatever was handy a few centuries ago. Inches, feet, pounds, gallons, Fahrenheit. Mostly used in the US.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how many cm in a meter'.

tutorials.title: Length Conversions
tutorials.body:
Metric: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm. Imperial: 1 mile = 5280 ft, 1 ft = 12 in. Bridges: 1 inch ≈ 2.54 cm, 1 meter ≈ 3.28 ft, 1 mile ≈ 1.609 km.

Example: 5 ft in cm. 5 × 12 × 2.54 ≈ 152.4 cm.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'convert 10 km to miles'.

tutorials.title: Weight Conversions
tutorials.body:
Metric: 1 kg = 1000 g. Imperial: 1 lb = 16 oz, 1 ton = 2000 lb. Bridge: 1 kg ≈ 2.205 lb, or 1 lb ≈ 0.454 kg.

Example: 150 lb in kg. 150 × 0.454 ≈ 68.1 kg.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'convert 70 kg to pounds'.

tutorials.title: Temperature Conversions
tutorials.body:
C to F: multiply by 9/5, then add 32. F to C: subtract 32, multiply by 5/9.

Example: 100°C in F. 100 × 9/5 + 32 = 180 + 32 = 212°F (boiling). 32°F in C: (32−32) × 5/9 = 0°C (freezing).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'convert 75 F to C'.

triggers: what does limit mean in math
tutorials.title: What Is a Limit (Intuition)
tutorials.body:
A limit asks 'what value is f(x) heading toward as x gets close to some number?' It's about the destination, not whether you arrive.

Example: as x → 2, x² → 4. Even if f(2) were undefined or weird, the limit can still be 4 — limits care about the trip, not the endpoint.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a derivative'.

tutorials.title: What Is a Derivative
tutorials.body:
The derivative of a function tells you its instantaneous rate of change — how fast it's rising or falling at each point. Geometrically, it's the slope of the tangent line at a point.

Example: if f(x) = x², then f'(x) = 2x. At x = 3, the function is climbing at a rate of 6 per unit of x.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'derivative of x³'.

triggers: what is rate of change in calculus
tutorials.title: Derivative as Instantaneous Rate of Change
tutorials.body:
Average rate of change over an interval is (Δy / Δx). The derivative is what you get when you shrink that interval down to a single instant.

Example: a car's average speed from minute 1 to minute 2 might be 60 mph. Its derivative at minute 1.5 is the exact speedometer reading right then.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'derivative as slope'.

tutorials.title: Derivative as Slope of Tangent
tutorials.body:
Draw a curve. At any point, the tangent line just barely touches the curve. The derivative at that point IS the slope of that tangent line.

This is why derivatives tell you whether a curve is going up (positive derivative), down (negative), or flat (zero — possibly a max or min).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the power rule'.

triggers: how to take derivative of x^n
tutorials.title: Power Rule
tutorials.body:
To differentiate x to a power: bring down the exponent as a multiplier, then subtract 1 from the exponent.

Examples: d/dx[x³] = 3x². d/dx[x⁵] = 5x⁴. d/dx[x] = 1. d/dx[constant] = 0.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'derivative of x^7'.

triggers: derivative of x to the n
how to differentiate x to a power
tutorials.title: Derivative of x^n
tutorials.body:
Works for any real exponent — positive, negative, fractional. d/dx[1/x] = d/dx[x⁻¹] = −x⁻² = −1/x². d/dx[√x] = d/dx[x^½] = ½·x^(−½) = 1/(2√x).

For polynomials, apply the rule term by term.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'derivative of 1/x'.

tutorials.title: Derivatives of Common Functions
tutorials.body:
Worth memorizing: d/dx[sin x] = cos x. d/dx[cos x] = −sin x. d/dx[e^x] = e^x (its own derivative). d/dx[ln x] = 1/x. d/dx[constant] = 0.

These plus the power rule cover most of intro calculus.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'derivative of sin x'.

tutorials.title: Chain Rule (Gentle)
tutorials.body:
For a function inside a function, differentiate the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.

Example: d/dx[(x² + 1)³]. Outside: u³ → 3u². Inside: x² + 1, derivative 2x. Answer: 3(x² + 1)² × 2x = 6x(x² + 1)².
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'derivative of sin(2x)'.

tutorials.title: Product Rule
tutorials.body:
Derivative of one times the other, plus the first times the derivative of the other.

Example: d/dx[x² · sin x] = 2x · sin x + x² · cos x.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'derivative of x times e^x'.

tutorials.title: Quotient Rule
tutorials.body:
Low-D-high minus high-D-low, over the square of what's below. Or memorize the formula directly.

Example: d/dx[x / (x+1)] = ((1)(x+1) − (x)(1)) / (x+1)² = 1/(x+1)².
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'derivative of sin x over x'.

tutorials.title: Antiderivative
tutorials.body:
An antiderivative of f is a function whose derivative is f. It undoes differentiation.

Example: an antiderivative of 2x is x², because d/dx[x²] = 2x. Also x² + 5, or x² − 7 — any constant works. So we write x² + C.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'antiderivative of x²'.

tutorials.title: Definite Integral
tutorials.body:
A definite integral measures the (signed) area under the curve of f from x = a to x = b. Areas above the x-axis count positive, below count negative.

If you know an antiderivative F, compute it as F(b) − F(a) (the fundamental theorem).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'integral of x from 0 to 2'.

tutorials.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
tutorials.body:
The grand link between derivatives and integrals: to find the area under f from a to b, find any antiderivative F and compute F(b) − F(a).

This is why calculus is one subject, not two. Areas and slopes turn out to be inverse operations.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'integral of x squared from 0 to 3'.

tutorials.title: What Is a Vector
tutorials.body:
A vector has both size (magnitude) and direction. Picture an arrow. In 2D you write it as a pair like (3, 4); in 3D it's a triple.

Vectors describe things like velocity, force, or displacement — any quantity that needs a direction along with a number.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how to add vectors'.

tutorials.title: Vector Addition
tutorials.body:
Add component-by-component. Geometrically, put the tail of the second vector at the head of the first — the sum runs from the very first tail to the very last head.

Example: (1, 2) + (3, 4) = (4, 6).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'add vectors (2, 3) and (5, 1)'.

tutorials.title: Dot Product
tutorials.body:
Multiply matching components, then add. The result is a single number (a scalar), not a vector.

The dot product also equals |u||v| cos(θ) where θ is the angle between the vectors. So zero dot product means they're perpendicular.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'dot product of (2, 3) and (4, 1)'.

tutorials.title: 2×2 Matrix Multiplication
tutorials.body:
Each entry of the result is the dot product of a row from the first matrix with a column from the second. Top-left = (row 1 of A) · (column 1 of B), and so on.

Example: [[1,2],[3,4]] × [[5,6],[7,8]] = [[19,22],[43,50]]. Order matters — AB usually doesn't equal BA.

tutorials.title: Determinant of a 2×2 Matrix
tutorials.body:
For a 2×2 matrix, the determinant is the cross-diagonal product: ad − bc. Geometrically, it's the area scaling factor of the matrix's transformation.

A zero determinant means the matrix squashes the plane onto a line — it has no inverse.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'determinant of [[1,2],[3,4]]'.

triggers: how to find inverse of 2x2 matrix
tutorials.title: Inverse of a 2×2 Matrix
tutorials.body:
Swap a and d, negate b and c, then divide everything by the determinant. If det = 0, no inverse exists.

Example: [[1,2],[3,4]]. Det = 4 − 6 = −2. Inverse = (1/−2) × [[4, −2], [−3, 1]] = [[−2, 1], [1.5, −0.5]].
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'inverse of [[2,1],[5,3]]'.

tutorials.title: Eigenvalue (Conceptual)
tutorials.body:
An eigenvector of a matrix is a special direction the matrix doesn't rotate — it only stretches or shrinks. The amount of stretching is the eigenvalue.

They show up everywhere: stability of systems, principal component analysis, quantum mechanics, vibrations of structures. They reveal a matrix's 'natural' axes.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'why are matrices used in graphics'.

tutorials.title: Why Matrices Matter
tutorials.body:
A matrix is a compact way to describe a linear transformation. Rotate, scale, project, shear — all are matrix multiplications.

That's why graphics engines use matrices to move 3D models, and why neural networks are giant stacks of matrix multiplies. Linear algebra is the math of 'transform a bunch of numbers at once'.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a vector'.

tutorials.title: Normal Distribution
tutorials.body:
The famous bell curve. Symmetric around the mean. Most values are near the middle; extreme values get rare fast.

68-95-99.7 rule: about 68% of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2, 99.7% within 3. Lots of real things (heights, errors, IQ) follow it roughly.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a z-score'.

tutorials.title: Z-Score
tutorials.body:
A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean. Positive = above average, negative = below.

Example: test mean 70, stdev 10. You scored 85. z = (85 − 70) / 10 = 1.5. You're 1.5 stdevs above average — top ~7% of test-takers.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the central limit theorem'.

triggers: what is the central limit theorem
tutorials.title: Central Limit Theorem (Plain Words)
tutorials.body:
If you take lots of random samples and compute the mean of each, those sample means form a roughly normal distribution — even if the original data is wildly non-normal.

That's why bell curves keep showing up. It's also why we can use normal-curve math to make confidence statements about averages.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a confidence interval'.

tutorials.title: Confidence Interval
tutorials.body:
A range of plausible values for a population parameter, based on a sample. '95% confident' means: if we repeated the whole survey many times, 95% of the intervals we'd build would contain the true value.

Example: a poll says 52% support a candidate, ±3% margin at 95%. The interval is 49% to 55%.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a p-value'.

tutorials.title: Hypothesis Testing (Intro)
tutorials.body:
Start with a 'null hypothesis' — usually 'nothing interesting is happening'. Collect data and compute how surprising it would be if the null were true.

If the result is very surprising (p-value below a threshold like 0.05), you reject the null and report evidence for the alternative. Otherwise you say 'not enough evidence' — never 'the null is true'.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a p-value'.

tutorials.title: P-Value (Conceptual)
tutorials.body:
A p-value answers: 'if the null hypothesis were true, how often would I see data as extreme as this just by chance?' Small p = the data would be surprising under the null.

By convention, p < 0.05 is often called 'statistically significant'. That threshold is a tradition, not a law of nature. p-values are about evidence, not proof.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a confidence interval'.

triggers: what is a set in math
tutorials.title: Sets
tutorials.body:
A set is an unordered collection of distinct things. Written with curly braces: {1, 2, 3}. Things in a set are called elements or members.

Order doesn't matter ({1,2} = {2,1}) and duplicates are dropped ({1,1,2} is just {1,2}).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is union and intersection'.

tutorials.title: Union, Intersection, Complement
tutorials.body:
Union (A ∪ B): everything in either set. Intersection (A ∩ B): only things in both. Complement (Aᶜ): everything NOT in A (relative to the universe you're working in).

Example: A = {1,2,3}, B = {2,3,4}. A ∪ B = {1,2,3,4}. A ∩ B = {2,3}.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what are de morgans laws'.

tutorials.title: Logic Operators (AND, OR, NOT)
tutorials.body:
AND (∧): true only if both are true. OR (∨): true if at least one is true. NOT (¬): flips true and false.

Example: 'is rainy AND cold' is true only when both. 'is rainy OR cold' is true if either holds. NOT rainy is true when it's not rainy.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a truth table'.

tutorials.title: De Morgan's Laws
tutorials.body:
Flipping NOT across AND/OR swaps them. 'Not (rainy and cold)' is the same as 'not rainy or not cold'.

Useful for simplifying logic, rewriting code conditions, and dealing with set complements.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a truth table'.

tutorials.title: Truth Tables
tutorials.body:
A truth table lists every possible combo of true/false inputs and shows the output. For two inputs, four rows. For three inputs, eight rows.

Example AND table: T∧T=T, T∧F=F, F∧T=F, F∧F=F. Only true when both inputs are true.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'truth table for or'.

tutorials.title: Big-O Intuition
tutorials.body:
Big-O describes how a program's running time grows as the input gets bigger. O(1) = constant (doesn't depend on size). O(n) = linear (doubles when input doubles). O(n²) = quadratic (4× when input doubles). O(log n) = grows slowly.

We only care about the dominant term as n → ∞, so we drop constants and lower-order terms.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is induction'.

tutorials.title: Induction (Plain Words)
tutorials.body:
Induction proves statements for all positive integers in two steps. Base case: show it works for n = 1. Inductive step: assume it works for n = k, then show it must work for n = k + 1.

Like dominoes: knock over the first one, then guarantee each one knocks over the next. All of them fall.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a recurrence relation'.

tutorials.title: Recurrence Relations
tutorials.body:
A recurrence defines each term using earlier terms. Like Fibonacci: F(n) = F(n−1) + F(n−2), with F(1) = F(2) = 1. So 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13...

They describe how sequences grow step by step. Closed-form formulas are sometimes available but the recursion is often clearer.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'fibonacci sequence'.

tutorials.title: Modular Arithmetic
tutorials.formula: a mod n = remainder when a is divided by n
tutorials.body:
Modular arithmetic is math on remainders. 17 mod 5 = 2 because 17 = 3·5 + 2. Two numbers are 'congruent mod n' if they have the same remainder.

Used everywhere: clock time, hashing, cryptography, parity checks. It's the math of cycling around.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is clock arithmetic'.

tutorials.title: Clock Arithmetic
tutorials.body:
A 12-hour clock is modular arithmetic mod 12. 5 hours after 9 is 2 o'clock, not 14 — you wrap around.

In math notation: (9 + 5) mod 12 = 2. Same idea works for days of the week (mod 7), bytes (mod 256), or any cycle.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '(15 + 22) mod 7'.

tutorials.title: Fermat's Little Theorem (Plain Words)
tutorials.body:
If p is a prime and a is not divisible by p, then a raised to (p−1) leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by p.

Example: p = 5, a = 2. 2⁴ = 16. 16 mod 5 = 1. Used in primality tests and in RSA cryptography.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is rsa'.

tutorials.title: Euclidean Algorithm
tutorials.body:
Fast way to find GCD. Replace the larger number with (larger mod smaller). Repeat until one number is 0; the other is the GCD.

Example: GCD(48, 18). 48 mod 18 = 12. Now GCD(18, 12). 18 mod 12 = 6. Now GCD(12, 6). 12 mod 6 = 0. GCD = 6.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'gcd of 252 and 105 using euclidean'.

tutorials.title: RSA at 10,000 Feet
tutorials.body:
RSA is public-key encryption built on number theory. You pick two huge primes, multiply them to get N. The product N is public; the original primes are secret.

It's easy to multiply primes but extremely hard to factor N back into them. Encryption uses public N. Only someone who knows the original primes can decrypt — that's the trick that secures most of the internet.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is prime factorization'.

tutorials.title: Infinitude of Primes (Euclid's Proof)
tutorials.body:
Suppose there were only finitely many primes. Multiply them all together and add 1. The result is not divisible by any prime on your list (always leaves remainder 1). So either it's a new prime, or has a new prime factor. Contradiction.

Conclusion: the list of primes never ends. Euclid wrote this proof over 2,000 years ago.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a prime number'.

tutorials.title: Adding and Subtracting Decimals
tutorials.body:
Line up the decimal points, then add or subtract column by column like normal whole numbers. Pad with zeros on the right if one number has fewer decimal places.

Example: 3.45 + 12.7. Rewrite as 3.45 + 12.70, stack with decimals aligned, add: 16.15.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me '5.6 + 2.84'.

triggers: what does power mean in math
tutorials.title: Exponents
tutorials.body:
An exponent says how many times to multiply a number by itself. 2⁴ means 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. The bottom number is the base, the small upper number is the exponent.

Special cases: x¹ = x. x⁰ = 1 (for any nonzero x). x² is 'x squared', x³ is 'x cubed'.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is 3 to the power of 5'.

tutorials.title: Rational and Irrational Numbers
tutorials.body:
A rational number can be written as a fraction of two integers. Their decimal expansions either stop or repeat. Examples: 1/2 = 0.5, 1/3 = 0.333..., 7 = 7/1.

Irrational numbers can't be written as a clean fraction. Their decimals go on forever without repeating. Famous examples: π, e, √2.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'is square root of 2 rational'.

triggers: how to turn a decimal into a fraction
tutorials.title: Decimal to Fraction
tutorials.body:
Write the decimal over its place value, then simplify. One decimal place → over 10. Two places → over 100. Three places → over 1000.

Example: 0.75 = 75/100 = 3/4. 0.6 = 6/10 = 3/5. 0.125 = 125/1000 = 1/8.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is 0.4 as a fraction'.

triggers: how to turn a percent into a decimal
tutorials.title: Percent to Decimal
tutorials.body:
Drop the % sign and move the decimal point two places to the left. That's the same as dividing by 100.

Example: 25% = 0.25. 7% = 0.07. 150% = 1.50.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is 8% as a decimal'.

tutorials.title: Midpoint Formula
tutorials.body:
The midpoint is the point exactly halfway between two points. Average the x's and average the y's.

Example: midpoint of (2, 4) and (8, 10) is ((2+8)/2, (4+10)/2) = (5, 7).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'midpoint of (0, 0) and (6, 8)'.
